interviewQuestions.question: What does it mean that a SwiftUI View is 'a function of state', and why does that matter practically?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It means the view's `body` doesn't hold pixels or mutate itself — it's a computed property that, given the current state, returns a description of what the UI should look like. The view struct itself is cheap and disposable; SwiftUI throws it away and recomputes `body` constantly, then diffs the new description against the old rendered tree and patches only what actually changed.

The practical fallout is everywhere once you internalize it. First, state can't live as a plain property on the struct — it would reset every time `body` reruns — so `@State` stores it in memory SwiftUI manages outside the struct's lifetime. Second, view identity (same conceptual view vs a new one) is inferred from structural position, not object identity, which explains why an innocuous refactor can silently reset state or break an animation. Third, performance is about how much of the tree has to re-evaluate on a given change, not about mutating fewer properties — which is why decomposing a giant `body` into smaller subviews is a real performance technique, not just cleanliness.

Most 'SwiftUI does something weird' bugs trace back to forgetting this model and reasoning about it like a mutable UIKit view instead.

**Testing:** whether you understand the declarative model deeply enough to predict its surprising behaviors, not just recite the phrase.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: You have a parent view with @State for a form's data, and three child views that each need to read and edit different fields of it. How do you structure the ownership?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
One owner, everyone else gets a binding. The parent keeps `@State private var form: FormData`, and it stays the single source of truth — I never let a child hold its own copy of the same conceptual data in a separate `@State`, because that's the fastest way to get two views silently drifting out of sync.

For each child that needs to *edit* a field, I pass a `@Binding` scoped to that piece: `$form.email` if the child just needs one field, or I break `FormData` into smaller pieces and bind each child to its own slice if the fields are logically separate. A child that only needs to *display* a value, not edit it, just gets the plain value passed in — no binding needed, since a binding implies write access the child doesn't use.

If the form gets complex enough — cross-field validation, submission state, network calls — I'd graduate `form` from a plain `@State` struct to an `@Observable` model object owned by the parent (or a view model), and pass that down by reference instead of threading individual bindings for every field. That's the point where Combine/Observation-based state management earns its complexity.

**Testing:** whether you default to single ownership with bindings, or reach for duplicated state that will drift.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Architecture

interviewQuestions.question: A list item's expand/collapse @State resets unexpectedly after a minor refactor — wrapping the row in a new container view. Why, and how do you fix it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
This is a view identity bug. SwiftUI infers identity mostly from structural position and type in the view tree — same type at the same position means 'this is the same view as before, keep its state.' Wrapping the row in a new container changes the structural shape of the tree at that position, so SwiftUI can conclude it's looking at a *different* view than before, even though visually it looks almost identical. A different view means its `@State` starts fresh — hence the expand/collapse state resetting.

To fix it, I'd first check whether the wrap actually needs to sit between the row and its stable identity, or whether the wrapping could happen *outside* the identity-bearing element instead. If the wrap is unavoidable, `.id()` is the explicit override — giving the row (or the wrapping container) an explicit stable identifier that survives the structural change, telling SwiftUI 'these are the same view across renders' regardless of what's around it.

The broader lesson I'd state out loud in an interview: SwiftUI identity is inferred, not declared, so any refactor that changes a view's type or position in the tree is a potential state-reset bug, and `.id()` is the tool for taking explicit control when the inference gets it wrong.

**Testing:** whether you can connect a vague symptom to the specific mechanism (identity inference), which is where junior engineers usually get stuck guessing.

interviewQuestions.question: Your team is deciding whether to rewrite an existing, working UIKit screen in SwiftUI, versus building new screens in SwiftUI going forward. How do you frame that decision?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd separate 'new work' from 'existing working code,' because the risk profile is completely different. For genuinely new screens, I default to SwiftUI — less boilerplate, easier previews, better accessibility defaults out of the box, and no legacy constraint pulling the other way. That's close to a free choice at this point in SwiftUI's maturity.

Rewriting an existing, working, well-tested UIKit screen purely to modernize it is a different call entirely. The cost is real (engineering time, regression risk on something users already depend on) and the benefit is often just aesthetic or morale-driven unless the screen specifically needs something SwiftUI does meaningfully better — fast iteration on a frequently-changing design, for instance. I'd want a concrete driver: a new design system rollout, a feature that needs SwiftUI-native capabilities, or a screen that's genuinely painful to maintain in UIKit — not 'SwiftUI is newer.'

The practical middle path most teams actually take is incremental: keep the UIKit shell and navigation, and drop new screens or new features in as SwiftUI via `UIHostingController`, using `UIViewRepresentable` in the other direction when a SwiftUI screen needs a mature UIKit component. That gets the velocity win on new work without betting the whole app's stability on a big-bang rewrite.

**Testing:** whether you can make an engineering trade-off argument instead of a framework-preference argument.
